   * chip-chart - https://chromanomicon.com/TestPatterns/

> The `*_yuv420p*`, `*_yuv422p*` comparison images made by `generate.sh` were converted to Y'CbCr and back with
> libswscale (`scale=in_color_matrix=bt709:out_color_matrix=bt709`). They therefore include any libswscale
> conversion error, and should not be used to validate libswscale. Use the `rp219/` references for that.

## SMPTE RP 219 reference bars (`rp219/`)

These are the reference images for testing RGB to Y'CbCr conversion. The aim is a reference that does not
depend on any ffmpeg colour conversion, so that ffmpeg's conversions can be tested against it.

| File | What it is | Made with |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `rp219_yuv444p10.mkv` | 10-bit 4:4:4 Y'CbCr, limited range, BT.709. The expected values. Lossless FFV1. | vapoursynth-colorbars |
| `rp219_yuv444p12.mkv` | 12-bit 4:4:4 Y'CbCr, limited range, BT.709. The expected values. Lossless FFV1. | vapoursynth-colorbars |
| `rp219_reference.vpy` | The VapourSynth script that generates the two files above. | |
| `validate_reference.py` | Checks the references against RP 219 and against the Resolve RGB bars. | |
| `smptehdbars_10_resolve.dpx` | 10-bit full-range R'G'B' bars. The source image for the RGB to Y'CbCr tests. | DaVinci Resolve |
| `smptehdbars_16_resolve.dpx` | 16-bit full-range R'G'B' bars. A control: a correct conversion matches the reference exactly. | DaVinci Resolve |
| `smptehdbars_8_from16.dpx` | 8-bit full-range R'G'B' bars, derived from the 16-bit DPX (`oiiotool smptehdbars_16_resolve.dpx -d uint8 -o smptehdbars_8_from16.dpx`, i.e. round(v x 255 / 65535)). Resolve's "8-bit" PNG render turned out to be 16-bit, identical to the 16-bit DPX. DPX rather than PNG, as oiiotool tags PNGs as sRGB, which ffmpeg would pick up. | oiiotool |

### Y'CbCr references (vapoursynth-colorbars)

[vapoursynth-colorbars](https://github.com/ifb/vapoursynth-colorbars) generates the bars from the
10-bit and 12-bit Y'CbCr values tabulated in SMPTE RP 219-2, so the expected values come straight from the
specification rather than from an RGB to Y'CbCr conversion.

The plugin is run with these options, which differ from its defaults:

* `iq=0` - the second patch of rows 2 and 3 is 100% white and 0% black instead of -I and +Q. Note the
  plugin's README lists the `iq` values the other way round (0 as 75% white, 3 as 100% white); the code
  uses 0 for 100% white and 3 for 75% white.
* `subblack=0`, `superwhite=0` - no below-black or above-white ramps on the bottom row.
* No edge shaping and no chroma subsampling. RP 219 calls for shaped bar transitions, and the plugin's
  examples blur the edges, but here every patch needs to be an exact 4:4:4 code value.

With these options every patch except the -2% PLUGE patch (Y'=46 at 10-bit, below black) has an exact
full-range R'G'B' equivalent, so an RGB source image can match it. -2%, -I, +Q and the ramps produce R'G'B'
values outside 0-1, and will need a floating point source instead.

To regenerate (needs VapourSynth, `brew install vapoursynth`, and a build of the plugin; the script loads it
from `~/git/vapoursynth-colorbars/.libs/libcolorbars.dylib`, edit the path to match yours):

```console
cd sourceimages/rp219
vspipe -c y4m -a bits=10 rp219_reference.vpy - | ffmpeg -i - \
    -vf "setparams=colorspace=bt709:range=tv:color_primaries=bt709:color_trc=bt709" \
    -c:v ffv1 -level 3 -slicecrc 1 rp219_yuv444p10.mkv
vspipe -c y4m -a bits=12 rp219_reference.vpy - | ffmpeg -i - \
    -vf "setparams=colorspace=bt709:range=tv:color_primaries=bt709:color_trc=bt709" \
    -c:v ffv1 -level 3 -slicecrc 1 rp219_yuv444p12.mkv
```

The references are stored as lossless FFV1 in Matroska (about 65 KB each, rather than 12 MB as `.y4m`), tagged
BT.709 limited range. Read them by decoding at their own pixel format (`-f rawvideo -pix_fmt yuv444p10le` or
`yuv444p12le`), so FFmpeg does no colour conversion; `validate_reference.py` shows how. If a tool needs them as
`.y4m`, `generate.sh` converts them.

To validate:

```console
python sourceimages/rp219/validate_reference.py
```

This checks:

* The 10-bit reference against the values published in RP 219: the 75% bars of the top row (e.g. 75% white
  is Y'=721, Cb=Cr=512), the 100% white patch of row 2 (Y'=940) and the -2%/+2%/+4% PLUGE patches
  (Y'=46/82/99). All match exactly.
* Both references against the BT.709 limited-range formula applied to the Resolve RGB bars below, over patch
  interiors. From the 16-bit DPX both match exactly; from the 10-bit DPX they are within 1 code value at
  10-bit and 2 at 12-bit, because 10-bit full-range RGB cannot hold every level exactly.

The 12-bit reference is only checked through the formula, not against the RP 219 12-bit table.

### R'G'B' source (DaVinci Resolve)

`smptehdbars_10_resolve.dpx` and `smptehdbars_16_resolve.dpx` are an independent RGB rendering of the same
bars, generated in DaVinci Resolve. Both are full range: 75% is 767 (0.75 x 1023) at 10-bit and 49151
(0.75 x 65535) at 16-bit, and 40% grey is 409 and 26214.

This was generated with Resolve 21, using the SMPTE Color Bar generator using the DaVinci YRGB colorspace. The timeline colorspace was Rec.709 (Scene) and written out with the RGB 10-bit and 16-bit.


Resolve's layout is not quite RP 219. Its bar edges differ from vapoursynth-colorbars by one pixel at some
boundaries (e.g. 239 vs 240), and its bottom-row PLUGE section sits about 68 pixels to the right, with the
-2% patch at 0% black since full-range RGB cannot go below it.

So tests that convert these DPX files and compare against the references should:

* compare patch interiors only, and exclude the bottom-row PLUGE section;
* expect an exact match from the 16-bit DPX;
* allow 1 code value from the 10-bit DPX (2 against the 12-bit reference), since 10-bit full-range RGB
  cannot represent every level exactly (75% is 767.25).

That makes the 16-bit file a control: if a converter is exact from 16-bit but not from 10-bit, the error is in
how it handles 10-bit input.

## Chroma siting chart (`chroma_siting_chart.png`)

A 16-bit RGB chart for checking chroma siting (chroma sample location): where each subsampled chroma sample
sits relative to the luma samples when converting to 4:2:2 or 4:2:0. Professional 4:2:2 (SDI, ProRes, DNxHD)
and H.264/HEVC 4:2:0 expect the chroma co-sited horizontally with the even luma samples; JPEG/MPEG-1 style
centres it between two luma samples. Getting it wrong shifts the colour half a pixel against the luma, with
nothing in the file to show it.

It is generated, so its values are exact, by:

```console
python sourceimages/make_chroma_siting_chart.py
```

1920x1080, full range, untagged (the PNG has no colour chunks, so FFmpeg reads nothing from it as frame
properties), mid grey with four bands of 270 rows:

| Rows | Content | Used for |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0-269 | Blue "tent": rises linearly to a peak exactly between columns 959 and 960, then falls. | Measuring horizontal chroma position. |
| 270-539 | The same, vertically, peaking between rows 404 and 405. | Measuring vertical chroma position (4:2:0). |
| 540-809 | Single-pixel vertical blue lines every 16 pixels: even columns in the left half, odd columns in the right half. | Checking the filter treats even and odd columns consistently; zoomed in, wrong siting shows as lopsided colour fringes. |
| 810-1079 | Single-pixel horizontal blue lines every 16 rows: even rows in the left half, odd rows in the right half. | The same, vertically. |

`tests/chroma_siting.py` converts it with each FFmpeg converter and reports where the chroma ended up; see the
script for the method.
